name: Dilithium-AVX512 (Optimized Vectorization Implementation of CRYSTALS-Dilithium)
workload: Dilithium2/3/5 and FIPS 204 ML-DSA KeyGen/Sign/Verify CPU cycle counts, median of 100,000 runs, single-threaded
claimed_speedup: AVX-512 vs AVX2: KeyGen +43.2%/+39.3%/+45.6%, Sign +36.6%/+41.6%/+43.7%, Verify +45.3%/+46.5%/+47.4% for Dilithium2/3/5 respectively; also reports NTT ~14x and INTT ~18x speedups over scalar C
hardware: Intel Core i7-11700F (Rocket Lake) @ 2.5GHz, Ubuntu 20.04, TurboBoost/Hyper-Threading disabled
tradeoffs: Requires AVX-512 with VBMI/BW/CD/VL/IFMA subsets (recent Intel/AMD only); repo has no LICENSE file or real README beyond the algorithm source and a speed-test harness (test/test_speed.c).
caveats: No LICENSE file, so redistribution terms are unclear even though the underlying algorithm (pq-crystals/dilithium) is CC0; repo has had no updates since 2023-07-18; numbers are the authors' own single-run benchmark (not independently reproduced by a third party), though code, compiler flags and CPU model are all public and I opened the repo and PDF this session.
found_via: arXiv search all:"signature scheme" AND all:"AVX2" -> arxiv.org/abs/2306.01989; code located via `gh search repos "dilithium avx512"`

name: Falcon-Mitaka GPU (High Throughput Lattice-based Signatures on GPUs)
workload: Falcon-512/1024 batched signature generation and verification throughput on GPU vs the AVX2-optimized CPU reference implementation
claimed_speedup: Falcon-512 on RTX 3080: 7.78x sign / 52.43x verify faster than AVX2 CPU; Falcon-1024: 20.56x sign / 148.56x verify faster than AVX2 CPU (Table 6); on A100, 20.03x/29.51x vs AVX2 (abstract)
compiler_and_flags: nvcc, GPU arch sm_86 (per repo Makefile, tested on RTX 3080 and A100); host-side AVX2 baseline compiler string was in a PDF table that did not extract cleanly and could not be fully confirmed
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 3080 (Ampere, 8704 CUDA cores) and A100 vs Intel Core i9-10900K CPU (AVX2 baseline)
tradeoffs: Needs a CUDA GPU and large signature batches to amortize kernel-launch overhead; single-signature latency is not necessarily better than CPU; public repo only ships Falcon-512 and Mitaka-512, not the 1024 variants benchmarked in the paper.
caveats: GPU-batch-vs-single-core-CPU comparison inflates the ratio, especially for verification (148.56x) which benefits from trivially parallel independent checks; treat the >50x verify numbers as a batching/hardware-class effect rather than a pure algorithmic win.
found_via: IACR ePrint search "GPU signature verification throughput" -> eprint.iacr.org/2023/399; repo link found inside the paper PDF text ("We open-sourced our implementation to https://github.com/benlwk/Falcon-Mitaka")

name: Code Generation of Faster Formally Verified NTT with Plantard Reduction
baseline: liboqs ML-KEM/ML-DSA NIST PQC reference C implementations (mlkem-native / mldsa-native)
workload: ML-KEM-512 decapsulation/encapsulation/keygen and ML-DSA-2 signing/verification/keygen CPU cycle counts; also isolated forward/inverse NTT cycle counts
claimed_speedup: End-to-end vs NIST PQC reference C: ML-KEM-512 decap +1.32x, encap +1.27x, keygen +1.17x; ML-DSA-2 sign +1.26x, verify +1.16x, keygen +1.11x; NTT-only 1.5x-1.8x forward, 1.7x-2.5x inverse; also 1.26x/2.19x over the formally verified formosa-mlkem Jasmin baseline on ML-KEM
hardware: Intel Xeon E-2314 @ 2.80GHz, 4 cores, TurboBoost/Hyper-Threading disabled
tradeoffs: Improves only the NTT component, not a full drop-in library; targets ML-KEM/ML-DSA/FN-DSA jointly from one code generator, so gains are shared but modest end-to-end (<1.3x for most operations).
caveats: 2026 preprint (IACR ePrint marks it 'Preprint', not peer-reviewed); paper states code is available at an anonymous.4open.science double-blind-review link, but that URL returned HTTP 401 when I checked it this session, so the repository could not be independently opened -- capped below Tier A on that basis even though CPU, compiler and methodology are fully stated in the PDF I did open.
found_via: IACR ePrint search "jasmin formally verified implementation performance" -> eprint.iacr.org/2026/1624

name: GOLF: GPU-accelerated Optimization for Lattice-based FALCON
baseline: FALCON reference implementation (the portable C backend bundled in liboqs)
workload: FALCON signature generation/verification throughput (ops/sec) on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 vs the single-core reference FALCON implementation
claimed_speedup: 42.02 kops/s signing, 10,311.04 kops/s verification on RTX 4090; 58.05x sign / 73.14x verify over the reference FALCON implementation; 7.17x/3.79x over the fastest prior GPU implementation
hardware: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (GPU side only); CPU model for the reference baseline is not stated in the abstract/page text I could access
tradeoffs: No public code repository located; batched GPU throughput number, not single-operation latency; needs large batches and a CUDA GPU to realize the claimed gains.
caveats: IACR ePrint marks this a 'Preprint' (not peer-reviewed); no code found via GitHub search; CPU baseline hardware and compiler flags not confirmed from the accessible page, and the >50x ratio with unstated baseline build flags means this is capped at Tier C per the implausible-ratio rule.
found_via: IACR ePrint search "GPU signature verification throughput" -> eprint.iacr.org/2025/749

name: GRASP: GPU-based paRallel Accelerated SPHINCS+
baseline: SPHINCS+ NIST reference implementation (the portable C backend bundled in liboqs)
workload: SPHINCS+ signing/verification throughput on GPU (CUDA) vs the NIST reference CPU implementation and vs prior GPU SPHINCS+ work
claimed_speedup: 1.37x-3.45x throughput vs state-of-the-art GPU-based SPHINCS+ solutions; more than three orders of magnitude (>1000x) over the NIST reference implementation
hardware: Not confirmed from the abstract/page text I could access (CUDA GPU, model unstated there)
tradeoffs: No public code repository located; GPU batch throughput vs single-thread reference, not representative of single-signature latency; SPHINCS+ is already the slowest NIST signature scheme so large multiples over its reference implementation are expected.
caveats: IACR ePrint marks this a 'Preprint' (not peer-reviewed); exact GPU model, CPU baseline, and compiler flags not extracted from the accessible page; the >1000x claim vs an unoptimized reference implementation is capped at Tier C per the implausible-ratio/unstated-methodology rule.
found_via: IACR ePrint search "GPU signature verification throughput" -> eprint.iacr.org/2024/1030
